Fiscal Policy

ECON 104

Fiscal Policy

Fiscal policy

Federal government policy on taxes, spending, and borrowing that is designed to influence business fluctuations.

Expansionary fiscal policy (shifts AD right)
  • Increased government spending (without increasing taxes)
  • Decreased taxes (without reducing spending)
  • Both generate deficits!
ECON 104
5

Why Should Fiscal Policy Work?

  • When the economy is at full employment, spending more won’t increase output.
  • New production will pull resources away from other sectors of the economy.
  • The increase in government spending will crowd out production by the private sector.
Crowding out

The decrease in private spending that occurs when government spending increases.

  • The government has to tax to spend.
  • If government borrows, it leads to increased interest rates, and people reduce investment spending.
  • The increase in government spending leads to increased prices, so people need to reduce their consumption.
ECON 104
6

Why Should Fiscal Policy Work?

ECON 104
7

Why Should Fiscal Policy Work?

  • If there is unemployment, then government spending can increase production.
  • The workers who earn money can also spend money now, and generate more production!
  • The additional increase in spending is due to the multiplier effect.
  • Fiscal policy can work because when resources are unemployed, the economy is operating inefficiently.
Multiplier effect

The additional increase in spending caused by the initial increase in government spending.

ECON 104
8

Why Should Fiscal Policy Work?

  • A decrease in consumer spending growth, ↓C, is equivalent to a decrease in velocity, ↓v.
  • AD shifts to the left.
  • The economy moves from a long-run equilibrium at point a to a short-run equilibrium at point b.
  • At point b, the economy is in a recession.
  • Because consumers want to hold more money, inflation decreases.
  • Because wages are sticky, real growth decreases.
ECON 104
9

Why Should Fiscal Policy Work?

  • If government does nothing, wages will adjust in the long run.
  • The economy will eventually return to its normal growth rate.
  • The government can offset ↓C by ↑G.
ECON 104
10

How Big Is the Multiplier?

  • Fiscal policy is much more successful when the multiplier is big.
  • The size of the multiplier is bigger when:
    • There are lots of unemployed resources.
    • The government can target spending on the unemployed.
    • Tax cuts go to people who want to spend immediately.
    • The government can tax savings.
    • Government borrowing doesn’t crowd out private consumption or investment.

Limits to Fiscal Policy

ECON 104
12

Crowding Out

The decrease in private spending that occurs when government spending increases.

  • The government has to tax to spend.
  • If government borrows, it leads to increased interest rates, and people reduce investment spending.
  • Increased government spending leads to increased prices, so people need to reduce their consumption.
ECON 104
13

Crowding Out

  • The debate over fiscal policy is about the balance of two opposing forces: crowding out versus the multiplier effect.
  • If additional government spending crowds out equivalent spending from the private sector, then the multiplier is zero.
  • If no amount of private sector spending is crowded out, the multiplier is 1.
  • If the increase in government spending causes additional private spending, the multiplier is greater than 1.
ECON 104
14

The Knowledge Problem

Fiscal policy is less effective when the government has difficulty figuring out which resources are unemployed and marshalling only those resources for its projects.

Government spending
  • If there are lots of unemployed dam workers and the government builds a dam, this will have a big multiplier.
  • But if there are lots of unemployed dam workers and the government builds an office building, this is likely to take resources used in office building construction from the private sphere.
  • Resources are heterogeneous (useful for different things) and they can’t costlessly be switched to other lines of production.
  • So the government spending on just anything during a recession won’t be helpful.
ECON 104
15

The Knowledge Problem

Tax cuts
  • Want to target tax cuts to people who will spend the money immediately, boosting AD.
  • But it’s hard to tell who will spend and who will save!
  • The poor are more likely to spend the money (creating a bigger multiplier) but poor people already don’t pay much in taxes, so targeting tax cuts to the poor is difficult.
  • If people expect tax cuts today to be matched by tax cuts in the future, they might just save the entire tax cut to pay off the later tax increase.

Higgs: Was the Wartime Boom Real?

Robert Higgs, “Wartime Prosperity?” (Journal of Economic History, 1992)

  • Output: official real GNP rose about 72% from 1939 to 1944. But war goods were bought at government-set prices (price controls, rationing), not market prices. Higgs’s adjusted GNP rose only about 5%.
  • Bullets as “output”: the accounts count military purchases as final goods, and even Kuznets’s fix counts durable munitions as capital. But a bullet fired is gone: 41 billion rounds of small-arms ammunition did not raise living standards.
  • Unemployment: 14.6% (1940) to 1.2% (1944), but 12 million people were in uniform, about 18% of the labor force.
  • Consumers and investors: real consumption per person fell over 6% from 1941 to 1943 (no new cars, rationing); real private investment fell 64%.
  • The real recovery came in 1946, as spending fell and controls ended: adjusted GNP +27%, consumption +18%. Higgs’s explanation: less “regime uncertainty” for private investors.

The Problem of Fiscal Policy

  1. Government needs to know how much spending or how much tax decreases will stimulate spending
    1. Don’t want to boost aggregate demand too much — this causes inflation
    2. Don’t want to boost it too little — this fails to boost growth
  2. To do this it needs to know the multiplier
    1. Needs to know which resources are idle
    2. Beyond that, it needs to know which resources are likely to remain idle
      1. Once they’re employed by the government, they can’t be employed by the private sector
  3. This assumes the government is better at finding uses for scarce resources than the private sector
  4. Also assumes a timely response by government…

The Problem of Fiscal Policy

ECON 104
20

The Timing Problem!

Fiscal policy is subject to many lags:

  1. Recognition lag: The problem must be recognized.
  2. Legislative lag: Congress must propose and pass a plan.
  3. Implementation lag: Bureaucracies must implement the plan.
  4. Effectiveness lag: The plan takes time to work.
  5. Evaluation and adjustment lag: Did the plan work? Have conditions changed?
What if by the time you realize you have to act, the problem has already worsened?
What if by the time you act, the economy is already recovering?

Automatic Stabilizers

Automatic stabilizers

Changes in fiscal policy that stimulate AD in a recession without the need for explicit action by policymakers.

  • Fiscal policy automatically changes to keep private spending higher during bad economic times.
  • When the economy is doing poorly:
    • Income, capital gains, and profits are all down, so everyone pays lower taxes.
    • More people apply for welfare, food stamps, and unemployment insurance.
  • Consumption smoothing and credit also act as automatic stabilizers.
ECON 104
22

Marginal Cost of Public Funds

  • How much is the cost to the economy of an additional $1 of money spent?
  • More than $1! Why?
    • Administrative and compliance costs — costs of paying government employees for collecting the money, tax filing costs (money and time).
    • Leakages in the system — corruption, bribes, etc.
    • Most important: taxes disincentivize people from working (this is the crowding-out effect!) — think about the effects of an increase in marginal tax rates!
ECON 104
23

Fiscal Policy and Real Shocks

  • What if there is a negative real shock causing the LRAS to decrease?
  • An increase in AD will cause inflation rather than growth!
ECON 104
24

What Happened During COVID

  • The COVID-19 pandemic was a real shock because it made it more costly for people to work together.
    • This shifted the LRAS curve to the left.
  • There was the additional problem that getting people back to work could make the pandemic worse.
  • Fiscal policy focused on temporarily protecting jobs and addressing the health costs of the pandemic.
  • Overall, the U.S. federal government spent more than $5 trillion on COVID-19 relief.

“Common Sense” Fiscal Policy

  • Ideal fiscal policy will increase AD by spending in bad times and reduce AD by taxing and paying off the bill in good times.
  • Makes both the busts and booms smaller and the economy less volatile.
  • Ideal fiscal policy is counter-cyclical because when the economy is down, the government should spend more, and when the economy is up, the government should spend less.
Counter-cyclical fiscal policy

Fiscal policy that runs opposite or counter to the business cycle — spending more when the economy is in a recession and spending less when the economy is booming.

ECON 104
27

Expansionary Fiscal Policy: Summary

ECON 104
28

Takeaways

Fiscal policy is most likely to be effective when:

  1. The economy needs a short-run boost, even at the expense of the long run.
  2. The problem is a deficiency in aggregate demand rather than a real shock.
  3. Many resources are unemployed and the fiscal stimulus, either tax cuts or expenditures, can be targeted to those unemployed resources.
  4. Government spending is efficient and productive.
  • The great debate over fiscal policy is about the balance of two opposing forces: crowding out versus the multiplier effect.
  • Ideal fiscal policy would be counter-cyclical — spending more in bad times and spending less in good times to offset declines and increases in private spending, respectively.
